On polynomial automorphisms of Nagata type

Huarcaya, Jorge A. C. 1 and Palacios, Joe 2,3 Address: 1 Universidad Nacional Mayor de San Marcos, UNMSM Address: 2 Universidad Nacional de Ingeniería, UNI Address: 3 Instituto de Matemática y Ciencias Afines, IMCA Email address: jcoripacoh@unmsm.edu.pe, jpalacios@imca.edu.pe
Abstract.

We define a family of polynomial ring homomorphisms generalizing the well-known Nagata automorphism. We establish necessary and sufficient conditions under which these homomorphisms are automorphisms, and verify that they satisfy the Jacobian conjecture. Additionally, we provide a necessary condition within this family to obtain wild automorphisms, and independently derive a property related to the upper semicontinuity of the Łojasiewicz exponent at infinity.

Key words and phrases: 
polynomial automorphisms, Nagata automorphism, wild automorphisms, linear PDE, Łojasiewicz exponent
2010 Mathematics Subject Classification
14R10, 13B25, 13F20, 35F05

1. Introduction

In what follows FF will be a field of characteristic 00 unless otherwise stated. The polynomials

(1) f⁡(x,y,z)=x−2​y​(z​x+y2)−z​(z​x+y2)2,g⁡(x,y,z)=y+z⁡(z​x+y2),h⁡(x,y,z)=z.\begin{split}f(x,y,z)&=x-2y(zx+y^{2})-z(zx+y^{2})^{2},\\ g(x,y,z)&=y+z(zx+y^{2}),\\ h(x,y,z)&=z.\end{split}

define an automorphism of F⁡[x,y,z]F[x,y,z] called Nagata automorphism [7]. The determinant of the Jacobian matrix of this automorphism turns out to be 11.

An automorphism is tame if it is a finite composition of elementary and linear automorphisms. An automorphism that is not tame is called wild [12].

In 1972, Nagata conjectured that the aforementioned automorphism is wild. This conjecture was proved in [12, Corollary 9].

In this work, we define a family of ring homomorphisms on F⁡[x,y,z]F[x,y,z], given in (2), generalizing the Nagata automorphism, which includes the family of automorphisms constructed by Bass [1] in some sense, but is quite different to the family of automorphisms constructed in [6, (1)]. Our family provides wild automorphisms under some assumptions, see Corollary 1. In Theorem 1, we solve a linear partial differential equation, whose solution is related to the non-vanishing of the Jacobian determinant of those automorphisms. As a consequence, we obtain a necessary and sufficient condition on homomorphisms of Nagata type with nonzero Jacobian determinant to be automorphisms, which is a particular case of the famous Jacobian conjecture, see Corollary 3.

Acknowledgments. We are grateful to Carles Bivià-Ausina for valuable comments on an early version of this article.

2. Nagata polynomial map

In the following paragraph we recall the notion of tame automorphisms of polynomials.

Fix a natural number n≥2n\geq 2. For each index 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n, the iith elementary automorphism of FnF^{n} on itself is the automorphism defined as

(x1,…,xn)↦(x1,…,xi−1,xi+f⁡(x1,…,xi−1,xi+1,…,xn),xi+1,…,xn),(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})\mapsto\Big(x_{1},\dots,x_{i-1},x_{i}+f(x_{1},\dots,x_{i-1},x_{i+1},\dots,x_{n}),x_{i+1},\dots,x_{n}\Big)\,,

where ff is a polynomial map in n−1n-1 variables, and its inverse is the automorphism

(x1,…,xn)↦(x1,…,xi−1,xi−f⁡(x1,…,xi−1,xi+1,…,xn),xi+1,…,xn).(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})\mapsto\Big(x_{1},\dots,x_{i-1},x_{i}-f(x_{1},\dots,x_{i-1},x_{i+1},\dots,x_{n}),x_{i+1},\dots,x_{n}\Big)\,.

It turns out that the Jacobian matrix of each elementary automorphism has determinant 11.

Since FF is an infinite field, there is a one-to-one correspondence between polynomial maps Fn→FnF^{n}\to F^{n} and nn-tuples of polynomials in F⁡[x1,…,xn]F[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]. In what follows, we shall focus on the case n=3n=3.

Definition 1.

For a polynomial φ∈F⁡[x,y,z]\varphi\in F[x,y,z], we set

(2) f⁡(x,y,z)=x−2​y​φ−z​φ2,g⁡(x,y,z)=y+z​φ,h⁡(x,y,z)=z.\begin{split}f(x,y,z)&=x-2y\varphi-z\varphi^{2}\,,\\ g(x,y,z)&=y+z\varphi\,,\\ h(x,y,z)&=z\,.\end{split}

The triplet (f,g,h)(f,g,h) induces an ring homomorphism on F⁡[x,y,z]F[x,y,z] which will be called Nagata homomorphism.

Note that (f,g,h)(f,g,h) is the identity when one takes φ=0\varphi=0, so (f,g,h)(f,g,h) may be seen as a perturbation of the identity. If φ=x​z+y2\varphi=xz+y^{2} then (f,g,h)(f,g,h) is the Nagata automorphism (1). If φ=λ⁡(x​z+y2)\varphi=\lambda(xz+y^{2}) with λ∈F\lambda\in F, then we obtain a family of automorphisms similar to those constructed by Bass [1], [5, 3.8.1].

The Milnor number of (f,g,h)(f,g,h) is the dimension

μ⁡(f,g,h)=dimFF⁡[x,y,z]⟨f,g,h⟩\mu(f,g,h)=\dim_{F}\frac{F[x,y,z]}{\langle f,g,h\rangle}

as vector space over FF.

Lemma 1.

If (f,g,h)(f,g,h) is a Nagata homomorphism, then μ⁡(f,g,h)=1\mu(f,g,h)=1.

Proof.

One has,

y\displaystyle y =(y+z​φ)−φ​z=g−φ​z,\displaystyle=(y+z\varphi)-\varphi z=g-\varphi z,
x\displaystyle x =(x−2​y​φ−z​φ2)+2​(y+z​φ)​φ−φ2​z=f+2​φ​g−φ2​z,\displaystyle=(x-2y\varphi-z\varphi^{2})+2(y+z\varphi)\varphi-\varphi^{2}z=f+2\varphi g-\varphi^{2}z,

hence we get an equality ⟨f,g,h⟩=⟨x,y,z⟩\langle f,g,h\rangle=\langle x,y,z\rangle of polynomial ideals, and this implies that μ⁡(f,g,h)=1\mu(f,g,h)=1. ∎

Remark 1.

Note that the Nagata homomorphism (f,g,h)(f,g,h) is not always an automorphism for any φ\varphi, despite the fact that μ⁡(f,g,h)=1\mu(f,g,h)=1 by Lemma 1. For instance, if φ=x\varphi=x, then (f,g,h)(f,g,h) is not an automorphism, because as a map (f,g,h)(f,g,h) sends both points (0,0,1)(0,0,1) and (−1,1,1)(-1,1,1) to (0,0,1)(0,0,1). Similarly, (f,g,h)(f,g,h) is not an automorphism for φ=y\varphi=y. In contrast, Corollary 3 provides a necessary and sufficient condition on φ\varphi, in order that its corresponding Nagata homomorphism (f,g,h)(f,g,h) is an automorphism.

Proposition 1.

The Jacobian matrix J⁡(f,g,h)J(f,g,h) of the Nagata homomorphism (f,g,h)(f,g,h), as in (2), has nonzero determinant in FF if and only if φ\varphi satisfies the linear partial differential equation:

−2​y​φx+z​φy=0.-2y\varphi_{x}+z\varphi_{y}=0\,.
Proof.

We have

fx\displaystyle f_{x} =1−2​y​φx−2​z​φ​φx,\displaystyle=1-2y\varphi_{x}-2z\varphi\varphi_{x},
fy\displaystyle f_{y} =−2​φ−2​y​φy−2​z​φ​φy,\displaystyle=-2\varphi-2y\varphi_{y}-2z\varphi\varphi_{y},
gx\displaystyle g_{x} =z​φx,\displaystyle=z\varphi_{x},
gy\displaystyle g_{y} =1+z​φy.\displaystyle=1+z\varphi_{y}\,.

(1−2​y​φx−2​z​φ​φx−2​φ−2​y​φy−2​z​φ​φyfzz​φx1+z​φygz001)\begin{pmatrix}1-2y\varphi_{x}-2z\varphi\varphi_{x}&-2\varphi-2y\varphi_{y}-2z\varphi\varphi_{y}&f_{z}\\ z\varphi_{x}&1+z\varphi_{y}&g_{z}\\ 0&0&1\end{pmatrix}

|1−2​y​φx−2​z​φ​φx−2​φ−2​y​φy−2​z​φ​φyz​φx1+z​φy|=1−2​y​φx+z​φy.\begin{vmatrix}1-2y\varphi_{x}-2z\varphi\varphi_{x}&-2\varphi-2y\varphi_{y}-2z\varphi\varphi_{y}\\ z\varphi_{x}&1+z\varphi_{y}\end{vmatrix}=1-2y\varphi_{x}+z\varphi_{y}\,.

If −2​y​φx+z​φy=0-2y\varphi_{x}+z\varphi_{y}=0 then the determinant of J⁡(f,g,h)J(f,g,h) is 11. Conversely, if the determinant of J⁡(f,g,h)J(f,g,h) is a constant c∈F−{0}c\in F-\{0\}, then

1−2​y​φx+z​φy=c.1-2y\varphi_{x}+z\varphi_{y}=c\,.

We give the following definition in order to determine the highest weighted homogeneous component of the polynomial φ=p⁡(x​z+y2,z)\varphi=p(xz+y^{2},z).

For k=(t1,…,tn)∈ℤ≥1nk=(t_{1},\dots,t_{n})\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}_{\geq 1}, we write tkt^{k} to denote the monomial t1k1⋯tnknt_{1}^{k_{1}}\cdots t_{n}^{k_{n}}.   1. (1)

    The support of hh, denoted by supp⁡(h)\mathrm{supp}(h), is defined as the set

    supp⁡(h)={k∈ℤ≥0n:ak≠0}.\mathrm{supp}(h)=\{k\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}_{\geq 0}:a_{k}\neq 0\}\,.
  2. (2)

    Let v=(v1,…,vn)∈ℤ≥1nv=(v_{1},\dots,v_{n})\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}_{\geq 1}. The degree of hh with respect to vv, denoted by dv​(h)d_{v}(h), is the maximum of the scalar product ⟨v,k⟩\langle v,k\rangle such that ak≠0a_{k}\neq 0. We denote by hvh^{v} the sum of those terms ak​tka_{k}t^{k} such that ⟨v,k⟩=dv​(h)\langle v,k\rangle=d_{v}(h). In particular, for v=(1,…,1)v=(1,\dots,1), we write

Proposition 3.

Let φ∈F⁡[x,y,z]\varphi\in F[x,y,z] and suppose that its corresponding Nagata homomorphism (f,g,h)(f,g,h) is an automorphism of F⁡[x,y,z]F[x,y,z]. If one the partial derivatives φ¯x,φ¯y\overline{\varphi}_{x},\overline{\varphi}_{y} is nonzero, then the automorphism (f,g,h)(f,g,h) is wild.

Proof.

Let f¯,g¯,h¯\overline{f},\overline{g},\overline{h} be the highest homogeneous component of f,g,hf,g,h, respectively. Since φ¯x\overline{\varphi}_{x} or φ¯y\overline{\varphi}_{y} is nonzero, we have deg⁡(φ¯)>0\deg(\overline{\varphi})>0, so

f¯=−z​φ¯2,g¯=z​φ¯,h¯=z.\begin{split}\overline{f}&=-z\overline{\varphi}^{2}\,,\\ \overline{g}&=z\overline{\varphi}\,,\\ \overline{h}&=z\,.\end{split}

f¯x​g¯y−f¯y​g¯x\displaystyle\overline{f}_{x}\overline{g}_{y}-\overline{f}_{y}\overline{g}_{x} =0\displaystyle=0

g¯x​h¯y−g¯y​h¯x\displaystyle\overline{g}_{x}\overline{h}_{y}-\overline{g}_{y}\overline{h}_{x} =0\displaystyle=0
g¯y​h¯z−g¯z​h¯y\displaystyle\overline{g}_{y}\overline{h}_{z}-\overline{g}_{z}\overline{h}_{y} =z​φ¯y\displaystyle=z\,\overline{\varphi}_{y}

f¯y​h¯z−f¯z​h¯y\displaystyle\overline{f}_{y}\overline{h}_{z}-\overline{f}_{z}\overline{h}_{y} =−2​z​φ¯y\displaystyle=-2z\,\overline{\varphi}_{y}

Therefore, by [12, Corollary 8] (f,g,h)(f,g,h) is wild. ∎

Lemma 2.

Let p∈F⁡[t1,t2]p\in F[t_{1},t_{2}] and v=(2,1)v=(2,1). If φ⁡(x,y,z)=p⁡(x​z+y2,z)\varphi(x,y,z)=p(xz+y^{2},z), then it is not always true that φ¯\overline{\varphi} coincides with p¯​(x​z+y2,z)\overline{p}(xz+y^{2},z). Corollary 1.

Let p∈F⁡[t1,t2]p\in F[t_{1},t_{2}] and set φ=p⁡(x​z+y2,z)\varphi=p(xz+y^{2},z) in F⁡[x,y,z]F[x,y,z]. If the partial derivative (pv)t1(p^{v})_{t_{1}} is nonzero, where v=(2,1)v=(2,1), then its corresponding Nagata homomorphism (f,g,h)(f,g,h) is a wild automorphism.

Proof.

By Proposition 2, (f,g,h)(f,g,h) is an automorphism and Lemma 2 establishes the equality φ¯=pv​(x​z+y2,z)\overline{\varphi}=p^{v}(xz+y^{2},z). Hence the fact that (pv)t1≠0(p^{v})_{t_{1}}\neq 0 implies that φ¯x≠0\overline{\varphi}_{x}\neq 0 and φ¯y≠0\overline{\varphi}_{y}\neq 0. By Proposition 3, the automorphism (f,g,h)(f,g,h) is wild. ∎

Since pv=t12+t1​t22p^{v}=t_{1}^{2}+t_{1}t_{2}^{2} and (pv)t1=2​t1+t12≠0(p^{v})_{t_{1}}=2t_{1}+t_{1}^{2}\neq 0, Corollary 1 implies that corresponding Nagata homomorphism (f,g,h)(f,g,h) is a wild automorphism.

Łojasiewicz exponent.— Let KK be a normed field. For z=(z1,z2,…,zm)∈Kmz=(z_{1},z_{2},\dots,z_{m})\in K^{m}, we write |z|=max1≤i≤m⁡|zi||z|=\max_{1\leq i\leq m}|z_{i}|. If F=(F1,F2,…,Fn):Km→KnF=(F_{1},F_{2},\dots,F_{n})\colon K^{m}\to K^{n} is a polynomial map, then we set deg⁡F=max1≤i≤n⁡deg⁡Fi\deg F=\max_{1\leq i\leq n}\deg F_{i}. The Łojasiewicz exponent at infinity of a polynomial map F:Km→KnF\colon K^{m}\to K^{n}, denoted by ℒ∞​(F)\mathcal{L}_{\infty}(F), is defined as the supremum of the real numbers α\alpha such that there exist two positive real numbers CC and RR so that

|F⁡(z)|≥C​|z|α|F(z)|\geq C|z|^{\alpha}

for all |z|≥R|z|\geq R in KmK^{m}. One can follow the argument provided in [11, (1.1)] to deduce that

(6) ℒ∞​(F)=1deg⁡(F−1)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\infty}(F)=\dfrac{1}{\deg(F^{-1})}

for every polynomial automorphism FF.

For K=ℝK=\mathbb{R} or K=ℂK=\mathbb{C}, it is well known that ℒ∞​(F)\mathcal{L}_{\infty}(F) exists if and only if F−1​(0)F^{-1}(0) is compact, and in this case, ℒ∞​(F)\mathcal{L}_{\infty}(F) is a rational number [8, Proposition 2.6]. The computation of this number is generally considered a highly nontrivial problem [4, 9, 11, 2, 3].

A polynomial deformation of a polynomial p⁡(t1,…,tm)∈K⁡[t1,…,tm]p(t_{1},\dots,t_{m})\in K[t_{1},\dots,t_{m}] is a polynomial H⁡(t1,…,tm,s1,…,sn)∈K⁡[t1,…,tm,s1,…,sn]H(t_{1},\dots,t_{m},s_{1},\dots,s_{n})\in K[t_{1},\dots,t_{m},s_{1},\dots,s_{n}] such that

H⁡(t1,…,tm,0,…,0)=p⁡(t1,…,tm).H(t_{1},\dots,t_{m},0,\dots,0)=p(t_{1},\dots,t_{m})\,.

For simplicity, we write s=(s1,…,sn)s=(s_{1},\dots,s_{n}), so that the polynomial ring K⁡[t1,…,tm,s1,…,sn]K[t_{1},\dots,t_{m},s_{1},\dots,s_{n}] shall be shortly written as K⁡[t1,…,tm,s]K[t_{1},\dots,t_{m},s], and this allows to set

ps​(t1,…,tm)=H⁡(t1,…,tm,s1,…,sn).p_{s}(t_{1},\dots,t_{m})=H(t_{1},\dots,t_{m},s_{1},\dots,s_{n})\,.

The following is motivated by the lower semicontinuous property of the Łojasiewicz exponent proven for finite holomorphic germs with constant Milnor number [10, Theorem 2.1]. However, for polynomial maps, we expect the upper semicontinuous property under certain conditions, in view of the fact that Nagata homomorphisms have a constant Milnor number, see Lemma 1.

Corollary 2.

Let ps​(t1,t2)∈K⁡[t1,t2,s]p_{s}(t_{1},t_{2})\in K[t_{1},t_{2},s] be a polynomial deformation of a polynomial p⁡(t1,t2)∈K⁡[t1,t2]p(t_{1},t_{2})\in K[t_{1},t_{2}]. Let φ=p⁡(x​z+y2,z)\varphi=p(xz+y^{2},z), φs=ps​(x​z+y2,z)\varphi_{s}=p_{s}(xz+y^{2},z), and suppose that (f,g,h)(f,g,h) and (fs,gs,hs)(f_{s},g_{s},h_{s}) are their corresponding Nagata automorphism. Then

ℒ∞​(fs,gs,hs)≤ℒ∞​(f,g,h)\mathcal{L}_{\infty}(f_{s},g_{s},h_{s})\leq\mathcal{L}_{\infty}(f,g,h)
Proof.

Since supp⁡(p)⊆supp⁡(ps)\mathrm{supp}(p)\subseteq\mathrm{supp}(p_{s}) with respect to the variables t1t_{1} and t2t_{2}, we have deg⁡(p)≤deg⁡(ps)\deg(p)\leq\deg(p_{s}), and for v=(2,1)v=(2,1) one has

deg⁡φ=dv​(p)≤dv​(ps)=deg⁡φs.\deg\varphi=d_{v}(p)\leq d_{v}(p_{s})=\deg\varphi_{s}\,.

Hence, in view of (6) we have

ℒ∞​(fs,gs,hs)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\infty}(f_{s},g_{s},h_{s}) =1deg⁡((fs,gs,hs)−1)\displaystyle=\dfrac{1}{\deg((f_{s},g_{s},h_{s})^{-1})}
=12​deg⁡φs+1\displaystyle=\dfrac{1}{2\deg\varphi_{s}+1}
≤12​deg⁡φ+1\displaystyle\leq\dfrac{1}{2\deg\varphi+1}
=1deg⁡((f,g,h)−1)\displaystyle=\dfrac{1}{\deg((f,g,h)^{-1})}
=ℒ∞​(f,g,h).\displaystyle=\mathcal{L}_{\infty}(f,g,h)\,.

∎

3. Statement of the main results

The main results in this work are the following:

Theorem 1.

The general solution in F⁡[x,y,z]F[x,y,z] of the linear partial differential equation:

(7) −2​y​φx+z​φy=0-2y\varphi_{x}+z\varphi_{y}=0

has the form φ=p⁡(x​z+y2,z)\varphi=p(xz+y^{2},z), where p∈F⁡[t1,t2]p\in F[t_{1},t_{2}].

Corollary 3.

Let φ∈F⁡[x,y,z]\varphi\in F[x,y,z] and let (f,g,h)(f,g,h) be its corresponding Nagata homomorphism as in (2). Then, the determinant of the Jacobian matrix J⁡(f,g,h)J(f,g,h) is a nonzero constant in FF if and only if (f,g,h)(f,g,h) is an automorphism of F⁡[x,y,z]F[x,y,z]. In this case, there exists a polynomial p∈F⁡[t1,t2]p\in F[t_{1},t_{2}] such that φ=p⁡(x​z+y2,z)\varphi=p(xz+y^{2},z), moreover the inverse of (f,g,h)(f,g,h) is given in (3).

The proofs of these results are given in Section 4. First of all, we shall provide some preliminary results in the next paragraphs.

Lemma 3.

Let φ=φ0+φ1+⋯+φn\varphi=\varphi^{0}+\varphi^{1}+\cdots+\varphi^{n} be a solution of the linear partial differential equation:

(8) A⁡(x,y,z)​φx+B⁡(x,y,z)​φy+C⁡(x,y,z)​φz=0,A(x,y,z)\varphi_{x}+B(x,y,z)\varphi_{y}+C(x,y,z)\varphi_{z}=0\,,

where each φk∈F⁡[x,y,z]\varphi^{k}\in F[x,y,z] is the homogeneous component of φ\varphi of degree kk for 0≤k≤n0\leq k\leq n, and A,B,CA,B,C are homogeneous polynomials of the same degree. Then each homogeneous component φk\varphi^{k} is also a solution of the equation (8).

Proof.

Replacing φ=∑k=0nφk\varphi=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\varphi^{k} into the linear PDE (7), we obtain:

∑k=0n(A⁡(x,y,z)​φxk+B⁡(x,y,z)​φyk+C⁡(x,y,x)​φzk)=0,\sum_{k=0}^{n}\Big(A(x,y,z)\varphi^{k}_{x}+B(x,y,z)\varphi^{k}_{y}+C(x,y,x)\varphi^{k}_{z}\Big)=0\,,

which is a sum of homogeneous polynomials of different degrees. Therefore,

A⁡(x,y,z)​φxk+B⁡(x,y,z)​φyk+C⁡(x,y,x)​φzk=0​for all​k=0,1,…,n,A(x,y,z)\varphi^{k}_{x}+B(x,y,z)\varphi^{k}_{y}+C(x,y,x)\varphi^{k}_{z}=0\,\,\,\textnormal{for all}\,\,k=0,1,\dots,n\,,

as wanted. ∎

By the previous lemma, to find the general solution of the equation (7), it is enough to deal with its homogeneous polynomials components.

Let φ∈F⁡[x,y,z]\varphi\in F[x,y,z] be a homogeneous polynomial of degree nn, if we consider the canonical isomorphism of rings F⁡[x,y,z]≅F⁡[x,y]​[z]F[x,y,z]\cong F[x,y][z], then we can suppose that φ\varphi has the form:

(9) φ=ϕn+ϕn−1​z+ϕn−2​z2+⋯+ϕ1​zn−1+ϕ0​zn=∑k=0n−1ϕn−k​zk+ϕ0​zn,\varphi=\phi^{n}+\phi^{n-1}z+\phi^{n-2}z^{2}+\dots+\phi^{1}z^{n-1}+\phi^{0}z^{n}=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\phi^{n-k}z^{k}+\phi^{0}z^{n}\,,

with ϕk∈F⁡[x,y]\phi^{k}\in F[x,y] homogeneous polynomials of degree kk for k=0,1,…,nk=0,1,\dots,n.

Lemma 4.

Let φ\varphi be a homogeneous polynomial in F⁡[x,y,z]F[x,y,z] of degree nn that is a solution of the linear PDE (7). Then, ϕn=a​yn\phi^{n}=ay^{n} and ϕ1=b​x\phi^{1}=bx, where aa and bb are constants in FF, and moreover

2​y​ϕxn−k−1=ϕyn−k2y\phi^{n-k-1}_{x}=\phi^{n-k}_{y}

for all k=0,1,…,n−2k=0,1,\dots,n-2.

Proof.

Let us derivate φ\varphi with respect to xx and yy:

φx\displaystyle\varphi_{x} =∑k=0n−1ϕxn−k​zk=ϕxn+∑k=1n−1ϕxn−k​zk,\displaystyle=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\phi^{n-k}_{x}z^{k}=\phi_{x}^{n}+\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}\phi^{n-k}_{x}z^{k}\,,

Substituting these equalities in the equation (7), we have

−2yϕxn+∑k=1n−1−2yϕn−kxzk+∑k=0n−2ϕn−kyzk+1+ϕ1yzn=0,-2y\phi_{x}^{n}+\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}-2y\phi^{n-k}_{x}z^{k}+\sum_{k=0}^{n-2}\phi^{n-k}_{y}z^{k+1}+\phi^{1}_{y}z^{n}=0\,,

and by index rescaling, we get

Hence,

This equation gives the equalities ϕxn=0\phi^{n}_{x}=0 and ϕy1=0\phi^{1}_{y}=0, so ϕn=a​yn\phi^{n}=ay^{n} and ϕ1=b​x\phi^{1}=bx for some constants a,b∈Fa,b\in F. Moreover,

The following result, will enable us to know how a solution can be written of the equation (7).

4. Proof of the main results

We are now ready to prove the main theorems.

Proof of the Corollary 3.

One implication is straightforward. Suppose that the determinant of J⁡(f,g,h)J(f,g,h) is a nonzero constant. By Proposition 1, φ\varphi satisfies the linear PDE (7). By Theorem 1, the solution of the equation (7) has the form φ=p⁡(x​z+y2,z)\varphi=p(xz+y^{2},z), where pp is a polynomial in F⁡[t1,t2]F[t_{1},t_{2}]. Finally, by Proposition 2, (f,g,h)(f,g,h) is an automorphism and its inverse is given in (3). ∎

5. Conclusions

In Corollary 3, we show that the Nagata automorphisms of the form (2) satisfy the well-known Jacobian conjecture. The proof is based on algebraic techniques for solving first-order linear partial differential equations. This result suggests a new strategy for approaching this longstanding open problem.
